title: Action at a Distance in Quantum Mechanics

summaries.example: Imagine two special coins made together and sent far apart. When one is checked, the other always shows the opposite result, even when no message could travel between them in time. Quantum experiments show correlations that are like this, although quantum particles are not ordinary coins.
summaries.summary: Quantum mechanics predicts unusual links between measurements made on particles that are very far apart. In an EPR/B experiment, each result may seem random by itself, but the two results can be strongly connected. Bell's theorem shows that, when common assumptions are accepted, no model that explains the results only through local causes at the particles' source can match all the quantum predictions. This leads many researchers to say that quantum physics involves some form of non-locality. The source explains, however, that people disagree about what this means. One interpretation treats a measurement as changing the distant particle's properties. Other views describe the particles as parts of one entangled system, or treat quantum mechanics mainly as a tool for predicting results. The entry also distinguishes non-local influence from faster-than-light signaling: the quantum links do not, according to the usual predictions, provide a controllable way to send information.
key_ideas: Experiments with pairs of particles reveal strong links between results at distant measuring stations.
Bell's theorem shows that local explanations using only a shared past cannot reproduce all the predictions of quantum mechanics, if certain reasonable assumptions hold.
Different interpretations of quantum mechanics explain the links in different ways. Some describe distant influence; others stress a shared, non-separate quantum state.
A faster-than-light connection does not automatically mean that people can send a useful message faster than light.
Philosophers ask whether quantum non-locality is action at a distance, a kind of wholeness, or something else.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic asks what a successful scientific theory tells us about reality. Quantum mechanics predicts results extremely well, but its distant correlations make us question whether objects always have fully separate properties. It also shows why careful definitions matter: influence, causation, entanglement, and communication are not automatically the same thing. Understanding these differences helps us discuss both physics and philosophy without jumping to conclusions.

important_terms.definition: A connection between results that is stronger or different from what we would expect by simply multiplying the separate chances of each result.
The idea that events or properties in far-apart places can be connected without a signal traveling between them.
A rule saying that the chance of two results together equals the chance of one result multiplied by the chance of the other.
A state in which a pair acts as one connected system, so the pair's properties cannot be fully described by describing each part separately.

questions_to_think_about: If two results are connected, must one cause the other?
Could a shared beginning explain every kind of connection between distant particles?
What is the difference between a strange connection and sending a message?
Can a pair be more than just two separate parts?

summaries.example: Consider two particles prepared in a spin-singlet state and sent toward distant laboratories. Each laboratory chooses an angle for its spin measurement. For the same angle, the results are perfectly opposite, while for different angles the pattern of joint results follows quantum probabilities. The laboratories can be space-like separated, so neither measurement lies in the other's ordinary light-cone. The correlations therefore cannot be explained by a simple local common-cause model that uses only the pair's earlier state and independent apparatus settings.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what quantum mechanics' distant correlations imply about locality, causation, and relativity. In EPR/B experiments, separated measurements produce correlations that are not represented by the product of their individual probabilities. Bell's theorem shows that, assuming empirical adequacy, independence between the source state and later settings, and a local factorizability condition, local common-cause models must satisfy Bell inequalities. Quantum predictions and experimental results violate those inequalities, so the source argues that some form of non-locality is widely accepted, while emphasizing that its exact nature remains disputed. Factorizability can be divided into parameter independence, concerning dependence on a distant setting, and outcome independence, concerning dependence on a distant outcome. The entry warns that this formal split may not by itself reveal the metaphysics of a theory. It instead compares interpretations: collapse theories, Bohm's theory, modal interpretations, and Everett-like approaches. These differ over action at a distance, holism, non-separability, and the status of measurement outcomes. The source also distinguishes superluminal causation from superluminal signaling. Standard quantum statistics prohibit controllable signaling, but this does not settle every question about alternative theories, hidden distributions, or relativity. Attempts to avoid non-locality through retrocausation, special correlations, detector inefficiency, or rejecting common-cause assumptions face their own challenges. The compatibility of quantum non-locality with special relativity therefore remains a subtle interpretive problem rather than a simple yes-or-no result.
key_ideas: Bell's theorem combines factorizability, independence between source states and apparatus settings, and empirical adequacy to derive Bell inequalities. Experiments support quantum predictions that violate those inequalities.
Factorizability splits into parameter independence and outcome independence. The source discusses whether these failures represent importantly different forms of non-locality.

Collapse theories can describe a measurement as producing an immediate change in distant properties. Bohmian theories use a non-local guiding structure, while other no-collapse interpretations give different accounts.
Entanglement motivates holism and non-separability: the pair may possess a correlational feature not reducible to separate properties of the particles.
Quantum mechanics rules out controllable faster-than-light signaling in its standard statistical predictions, although the broader question depends on the details of an interpretation or theory.

Whether quantum non-locality is compatible with special relativity depends on what relativity is taken to prohibit: all superluminal influence, signaling, or only structures incompatible with relativistic spacetime.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because quantum theory forces a separation between several ideas often treated as equivalent: correlation, causation, action at a distance, separability, and communication. Bell's result limits the possibility of explaining quantum correlations through ordinary local common causes, but it does not by itself select one interpretation of quantum mechanics. Studying the competing analyses clarifies what a physical theory commits us to and why matching experimental predictions may not settle questions about ontology. It also shows how foundational physics connects mathematical probability with broader philosophical questions about reality and spacetime.

important_terms.definition: The condition that the joint probability of two distant outcomes equals the product of their separate probabilities, given a more complete state and the measurement settings.
The condition that a distant outcome's probability does not depend on the nearby measurement setting.
The condition that a distant outcome's probability does not depend on the outcome obtained nearby.
A theorem showing that local models satisfying relevant assumptions obey Bell inequalities, which quantum predictions violate.
A feature of a composite system whose properties are not fixed by the intrinsic properties of its parts and their spacetime relations alone.
The failure of the state of a composite system to be wholly determined by separate states of its subsystems.
A distant change in intrinsic properties produced without a continuous process carrying the influence through space and time.
A dependence or influence faster than light; it need not be usable to transmit information.

questions_to_think_about: Does violating outcome independence by itself establish non-separability, or are additional locality assumptions needed?
Why might parameter dependence suggest a greater risk of faster-than-light signaling than outcome dependence?
Can a theory contain non-local correlations without allowing controllable communication?
Should a change in knowledge count as a physical change in the distant system?
What should count as a genuinely relativistic theory: correct observable predictions, or relativistic structure at the level of individual processes?

summaries.example: Suppose a machine sends two linked particles to two different classrooms. Each class chooses how to test its particle. A single result looks random, but when the classes compare notes, their results fit a precise pattern. The classrooms may be so far apart that light could not carry a message from one test to the other. A natural thought is that the particles carried matching instructions from the machine. Bell's theorem shows that local instruction-based explanations cannot reproduce every quantum prediction if the experimenters' choices are independent of the particles' earlier state.
summaries.summary: Quantum mechanics predicts striking correlations between measurements on distant particles. In an EPR/B-style experiment, a pair is prepared together and sent in opposite directions. Each measurement result appears random, yet the results match a precise pattern, including perfect opposite results when the same direction is measured. Because the measurements can be separated so that light cannot travel between them in time, the correlations raise a question about locality. Could the particles simply have received a complete set of instructions at their common source? Bell's theorem says that local models of this kind, under assumptions about factorization, independent measurement settings, and agreement with quantum predictions, must satisfy Bell inequalities. Experiments support the quantum predictions instead. Many philosophers and physicists therefore accept that quantum theory involves some kind of non-locality, but they disagree about what kind. Factorizability can be divided into parameter independence, which concerns the effect of a nearby apparatus setting on a distant result, and outcome independence, which concerns the effect of a nearby result on the distant result. The source explains why neither simple label completely settles the philosophical issue. Different interpretations describe collapse, hidden variables, holistic states, relational properties, or branching structures. The entry also asks whether these connections imply superluminal causation or action at a distance. It stresses that standard quantum mechanics does not permit controllable superluminal signaling, even though its correlations are non-local in an important sense.
key_ideas: The EPR/B experiment involves distant measurements whose outcomes are individually uncertain but jointly correlated.
Bell's theorem challenges the idea that all the correlations can be explained by local information stored when the particles were created.
Factorizability has two parts: parameter independence and outcome independence. Philosophers disagree about whether these parts capture the important meaning of locality.
Some interpretations say a measurement changes a distant system; others describe one entangled state, guiding fields, relative properties, or other structures.
Non-locality is not the same as sending a message faster than light. Standard quantum predictions do not allow a controllable faster-than-light telephone.
The relationship between quantum mechanics and special relativity depends partly on what kinds of superluminal influence relativity forbids.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it tests what we mean by locality and by explanation. A theory may predict connected distant outcomes without offering a way to control those outcomes or send information. The discussion also shows that a mathematical condition such as factorizability can be interpreted in several philosophical ways. Learning these distinctions helps students understand why a scientific theory can be successful while still leaving open deep questions about what the world is like.

important_terms.definition: A special connection between the results of measurements on systems that were prepared together, even after the systems are separated.
The view that distant systems or events can have influences or connections that are not carried by signals moving through nearby space.
The idea that a joint chance equals the product of the separate chances, once the relevant earlier state and settings are specified.
A result showing that local common-cause models obey Bell inequalities, while quantum mechanics predicts violations of them.
The idea that a whole system can have properties not fixed by the properties of its parts and the relations between them.
The idea that a composite system's state cannot be fully built from separate states belonging to its parts.
A proposed influence between distant systems without a continuous signal or process traveling through the space between them.

questions_to_think_about: If two events are correlated, does one have to cause the other?
Why is a shared past not enough to explain every quantum correlation?
What is gained by separating parameter independence from outcome independence?
Can a theory be non-local but still prevent faster-than-light messages?
Would changing someone's knowledge count as changing a distant object's physical properties?
